column1: # Curated SEC filer decisions for the MONEY layer, and the refusals.
# WHY TICKERS AND NOT CIKs
# A CIK is the identifier that matters, and it is NOT written here,
# because every CIK in this file would be one I typed from memory. The
# ingester resolves ticker -> CIK from EDGAR's own
# https://www.sec.gov/files/company_tickers.json and then confirms the
# company's name and SIC from its submissions file. Identity comes from
# the source, never from a guess.
# WHY A FILE AND NOT A TABLE
# Same reason as org_aliases.tsv: a curated judgement belongs where it
# shows up in a diff, not where it can be UPDATEd at 2am (AD-052).
# WHY NO NAME MATCHING
# EDGAR gives a stable numeric identifier. Matching company names to
# `organizations` is strictly worse than mapping a CIK by hand once --
# and 2026-10-12 spent most of a morning on what name matching costs
# (AD-108, AD-110). org_code is decided by a person who has read the
# survey output, never inferred.
# decision: pending -> --apply REFUSES the row. The survey has not been
#                      read and no org_code has been chosen yet.
#           match   -> write claims, link to org_code
#           claim   -> write claims with NO org_code. The company is a
#                      real filer whose money we want; `organizations`
#                      simply has no row for it, and AD-085 says the
#                      link is an attribute rather than a requirement.
#           refuse  -> no claims. Say why.
# Every ticker below is UNVERIFIED until `--survey` prints EDGAR's own
# name and SIC beside it. Tickers are easier to be right about than
# CIKs, which is the whole reason this column is tickers.
ticker
LMT
column4: Lockheed Martin. SIC expected 3760/3761. organizations has LM; confirm against the survey before matching.

column1: NOC
column4: Northrop Grumman. GCAT models the business units and may have no parent row - 10-12 found exactly that. Expect `claim` rather than `match`.

column1: BA
column4: Boeing. organizations has BOE (Boeing Co.), the parent, as of the 10-12 re-match. Confirm.

column1: RTX
column4: RTX (Raytheon). organizations has RAYTH = "Raytheon Space and Information Systems", a BUSINESS UNIT. A filer's revenue is the enterprise's; coding it to a unit would be AD-101's defect. Expect `claim`.

column1: LHX
RKLB
column4: Rocket Lab. A pure-play launch operator, so GCAT very likely has it.

column1: ASTS
column4: AST SpaceMobile. Direct-to-cell constellation operator, so GCAT plausibly has a row; a heavy R&D filer, which is the metric this source is best at.

column1: PL
column4: Planet Labs. An imagery operator with a large fleet, so GCAT almost certainly has it. Watch the fiscal year: Planet's FY ends in January, so FY labels lag the calendar.

column1: SPIR
column4: Spire Global. Smallsat operator; also restated financials in 2024, which makes it the useful test of whether a later filing supersedes an earlier one on the same period end.

column1: BKSY
column4: BlackSky. Imagery operator. Small revenue base, so a quarterly fact mistaken for an annual one would be glaring rather than subtle - a good canary for the fp=FY filter.

column1: MNTS
column4: Momentus. May have delisted; the survey will say.

column1: RDW
column4: Redwire. Space infrastructure manufacturer rather than an operator, so GCAT may have no row at all; expect 'claim' rather than 'match'.

column1: LUNR
column4: Intuitive Machines. Lander developer, NASA CLPS contractor - so it should also appear in the USAspending claims, which makes it a candidate for a cross-source comparison.

column1: VSAT
column4: Viasat. Satellite communications operator, and large enough that its revenue dwarfs the pure-plays; useful for checking the resolver does not mix scales within one metric.

column1: IRDM
column4: Iridium. Constellation operator with a long filing history, so it should give the deepest annual series of any filer in this seed.

column1: GSAT
column4: Globalstar. organizations has GLOB, which won its collision on name_native. Confirm.
